Here's an actual one with a very strange story behind it; Joe Flynn's Personal Eggs.

Joe Flynn was a Hollywood actor most remembered for playing the role of the bumbling Capt. Binghampton in the 1960s TV show McHale's Navy. As a hobby, he raised chickens in the backyard of his Burbank home and became popular among the community of stars for his invitation-only breakfast events. The eggs from his chickens were said to be so exceptionally delicious that celebrities competed with each other for a chance to attend his breakfasts and try them. Soon, the demand was so great that Flynn was convinced to go into business raising chickens and providing them daily by door-to-door delivery, and so was born Joe Flynn's Personal Eggs. Marlon Brando was a particular fan and was soon featured in advertising

Even as Flynn's TV career continued, the egg business proved very successful, so much so that it still proved difficult to meet demand. Flynn wanted to find ever-better ways of providing these eggs to his celebrity customers and so invented this strange idea of providing pre-shelled eggs on-tap in people's homes. You would literally have this refrigerated tank in your home hooked up to a special sink tap, right next to the kitchen sink, supplying you with raw eggs on demand. The tank would be refilled by a refrigerated truck and hose every week. Flynn hired an engineer to develop the system and his celebrity friends eagerly signed up, with Brando being one of the first to get the system installed.

Unfortunately, this eggs on tap system was a complete failure. The machinery was chronically failure prone, resulting in clogs, leaks, and the foul stench of rotting eggs filling people's homes. Brando was so annoyed with the thing he filled the tank up with concrete and never touched it again. A wave of high-profile lawsuits came down on Joe Flynn's Personal Eggs, just as Flynn's own film and TV career were beginning to wane. Financially ruined, the story ended as so many Hollywood stories do, with Flynn found one day naked and dead on the bottom of his swimming pool. And so ended the saga of Joe Flynn's Personal Eggs.

Anyway, [Nichijou ](https://veuwer.com/i/3ujh.jpg)is for all intensive purposes a slice of life comedy. Now before I start discussing what makes Nichijou great and subversive from other counterparts in the genre of slice of life, I want to explain how I feel about the genre as a whole. For me, most slice of life is not that great, but that is more to do with the direction and just blatantly bad writing that most slice of life or just sitcoms in general suffer from than any lack of taste for the genre. I've seen plenty of great shows that would be classified as a slice of life: Azumanga Daioh, Lucky Star, Barakamon, all shows that seem to have an excessive understanding of what a lovable little shit is... [aka character.](https://veuwer.com/i/3ujk.png)

The issue that I have with the average slice of life and sitcom is that they put excessive effort into trying to make the viewer laugh, to the point that I consider it distracting. That jokes and situations are made to be absurd to try and get a reaction out of the viewer without any actual thought or reason placed into the event itself. [ "Oh no, the main character has fallen into the tits of the shy girl, what a ridiculous set of circumstances,"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=sf-VVBrRbJY) roll laugh track, and repeat to keep the viewer from ever really even ingesting the content they are shown. That the events are less for the viewer to think about and more for the viewer just say, "wow, how crazy/silly". And at first glance, Nichijou gives off this same feeling "oh look how absurd this is". However, I can reassure that it makes up for it simply by making a point with its absurdity.

Ever sit there watching a comedy and see something ridiculous happen and ask yourself, "sure that is insane, but that would never happen"? It is a problem I feel plagues most casual comedy, and Nichijou circumvents this simply by not doing it. Instead, Nichijou is about taking otherwise normal, relatable events and cranking the absurdity of the characters interactions to 11. The show isn't about people being stuck in ever increasingly or incredible situations and instead takes otherwise normal situations that the average human experiences and puts them through a lens of absurdity that the viewer can still relate to.

My friend probably put it best, but his view on Nichijou is it is a show about how ordinary life is, through the absurd lens of anime. And I would agree with it. This is also punctuated by the shear level of craft and polish the show has. Something can be presented as "absurd" for all intensive purposes, but the pure production value that goes into scenes like the: ([mind you this happens in the first episode](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XnGv-lOg2a8)) are what make Nichijou stand above and beyond as a comedy animation.

Which is a big part of what makes the show so funny. It's humor is relatable, absurd, and almost entirely conveyed through the animation itself. There are not many things that uses its animation to such comedic effect that I have seen. Couple that with a truly lovable cast of adorable shitheads, a pretty modest amount self awareness of being an anime, some interjections purely for introspection and pondering on the viewer's part, an almost literal representation of daydreaming, and some honest themes about how absurd normal life is, you're left with probably one of the best feel good animes out there.

That's not to say Nichijou has its faults, some characters didn't get as much screen time as I would have hoped and sometimes the jokes are a bit obtuse especially if you aren't familiar with japanese humor (guilty of that myself). But if you want a show that is incredibly animated, that will have you laugh hysterically every single episode, as well as just a well of great reaction pics and gifs, Nichhijou is one of the best, if not the best anime for that.

It's good. Damn good. And one of those few shows that understand that absurdity is not funny just for the sake of being funny. The show feels like a fun afternoon of daydreaming, of what it would have been like to react differently to that one thing that happened to you. Or how the average person does overthink their otherwise normal lives. Or how the extraordinary or differentiating things about your body or personality just add to the absurdity of our otherwise normal lives, and make for something more normal. It is a show about no matter how absurd your life is, how life itself is, it is normal. It is a show, at it's core about depicting normal, every day life. And I believe that, because they accomplish that.
